name: Pharaonic Egyptian state
date_note: c.; conventional unification to Macedonian conquest; Seshat splits it into period polities (Old, Middle, New Kingdom, Late Period)
making_significance: Royal and temple workshops organised stone, metal, faience, linen and papyrus production at state scale for nearly three millennia.
materials_techniques: stone carving; faience; lost-wax copper-alloy casting; linen weaving; papyrus making; gold working
object_types: statues; reliefs; coffins; jewellery; linen; papyri
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Egyptologists; Manetho's king-list (3rd c. BCE); the state's own king-lists
leaves_out: mostly anonymous workers (Deir el-Medina a rare named exception); conscripted and enslaved labour; Nubian, Libyan and Levantine neighbours and captives; intermediate periods; present-day Egyptians' relation to the past
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Brooklyn Museum (CC BY where marked);British Museum collection search (link out);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Dynasties grouped as DYN rows; funerary material hidden by default; many museum objects left Egypt under colonial-era partage and dealing.

name: Kingdom of Kerma
making_significance: Kerma's workshops made thin-walled black-topped red beakers and faience inlays and built mud-brick deffufa temples.
materials_techniques: handmade ceramics; faience; mud-brick architecture; mica cut-outs
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;shelter;food and storage
defined_by: archaeologists (Reisner, Bonnet); Egyptian texts naming Kush
leaves_out: Egyptian hostile framing of Kush; retainers buried in royal tumuli; pastoralist neighbours; present-day Sudanese communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Reisner's early interpretations (Egyptian governors) were overturned; check museum captions.

name: Kingdom of Kush (Napata and Meroë)
date_note: c.; Napatan phase to c. 300 BCE, Meroitic to c. 350 CE
making_significance: Kushite rulers built pyramid fields and temples and Meroë smelted iron and wrote in its own Meroitic script.
materials_techniques: iron smelting; sandstone building; gold working; painted ceramics; Meroitic script
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing;tools
defined_by: Egyptologists and Sudan archaeologists; Kushite royal inscriptions
leaves_out: non-royal Meroitic makers; enslaved and conscripted labour; Blemmyes and other neighbours; Sudanese communities today
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);British Museum collection search (link out);Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Ferlini's 1834 destruction of Amanishakheto's pyramid (jewellery in Berlin and Munich). Scale of Meroitic iron industry debated.

name: Makuria
date_note: c.; absorbed Nobadia by 7th c.; decline 14th–15th c.
making_significance: Makurian churches such as Faras carried painted murals, and Nubian workshops produced a distinctive painted pottery.
materials_techniques: tempera wall painting; wheel-made painted ceramics; mud-brick and stone building; Old Nubian writing
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;record and writing;food and storage
defined_by: excavation teams (Polish mission); Arabic sources on the baqt treaty
leaves_out: people sent north as tribute under the baqt; Nobadian and Alodian neighbours; non-Christian pastoralists
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Faras murals split between Warsaw and Khartoum after 1960s UNESCO campaign.

name: Mahdist State
making_significance: The Mahdist state standardised the patched jibba tunic, banners and weapons, many of which entered museums as 1898 battlefield trophies.
leaves_out: Sudanese families of the dead; enslaved people within the state; the Omdurman loot's route into collections
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Many "Mahdist" objects in UK museums are war loot from Omdurman.

name: Kingdom of Aksum
making_significance: Aksum carved monolithic stelae, minted gold, silver and bronze coins and adopted Christianity under Ezana in the 4th century.
materials_techniques: monolith quarrying and carving; coin minting; Ge'ez writing
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value;record and writing
defined_by: historians; Periplus of the Erythraean Sea; Aksumite inscriptions
leaves_out: labour that quarried and moved stelae; Beja and other neighbours; Himyarite subjects during Aksumite rule in Yemen
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out);open-access excavation reports
notes: Stela taken to Rome 1937, returned 2005.

name: Ethiopian Empire (Solomonic)
making_significance: The Solomonic court and church patronised illuminated manuscripts, icon painting and processional crosses across seven centuries.
materials_techniques: parchment manuscripts; tempera icon painting; cast and forged crosses; woven and embroidered textiles
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Ethiopian royal chronicles and the Kebra Nagast; historians
leaves_out: Muslim, Oromo, Beta Israel and southern peoples incorporated by conquest; enslaved people; objects taken at Maqdala 1868
free_sources: Walters Art Museum (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0);British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Solomonic dynasty is the same ruling house (no separate DYN row). Tabots are sacred and never displayed.

name: Adal Sultanate
making_significance: Adal's centre Harar was walled in the 16th century and became a city of manuscripts and basketry.
materials_techniques: stone and lime building; manuscript copying; coiled basketry
leaves_out: pastoralist Somali and Afar communities; women basket-makers of Harar
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Library Endangered Archives Programme (link out; terms vary)
notes: Harar basketry is documented mostly for later periods.

name: Kilwa Sultanate
date_note: c.; traditional founding c. 10th c.; Portuguese sack 1505
making_significance: Kilwa minted copper coins and built coral-stone mosques and the Husuni Kubwa palace set with imported ceramics.
materials_techniques: coral-stone building; coin minting; imported ceramics used as architectural inlay
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;ritual and belief;shelter
leaves_out: enslaved people traded; mainland gold and ivory producers; non-elite Swahili townspeople
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Mahdali dynasty is a DYN row.

name: Swahili city-states of the Lamu archipelago and Kenya coast
date_note: c.; each city had its own chronology
making_significance: The Swahili towns produced carved wooden doors, coral-stone houses, furniture and manuscripts at the meeting of African, Arabian and Indian Ocean trades.
materials_techniques: coral-stone building; woodcarving; plasterwork; manuscript copying
object_types: carved doors; chairs; plaster niches; manuscripts
functions: shelter;rule and display;exchange and value;record and writing
leaves_out: enslaved plantation workers; mainland Mijikenda and others; women's craft
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);open-access excavation reports
notes: Debated as one "polity": a grouping of rival city-states.

name: Sultanate of Zanzibar
making_significance: Zanzibar's court and merchants commissioned carved doors, palaces and clove-plantation wealth built on enslaved labour.
leaves_out: enslaved people (slave market to 1873) and plantation workers; mainland caravans
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)
notes: Link to Omani state row.

name: Kingdom of Buganda
date_note: c. 14th c. start; abolished 1966, restored as a cultural kingdom 1993
making_significance: Buganda's royal court organised barkcloth making and built the Kasubi royal tombs in thatch.
materials_techniques: barkcloth beating; thatch architecture; drum making
functions: rule and display;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;shelter
defined_by: Ganda court historians; Apolo Kagwa; historians
leaves_out: non-Ganda neighbours raided and subjected; bakopi commoners
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)
notes: Ugandan barkcloth making is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list (2008).

name: Kingdom of Rwanda
making_significance: The Rwandan court patronised fine coiled basketry and the imigongo cattle-dung painted panels linked to the east of the kingdom.
leaves_out: colonial racial categorisation of Hutu, Tutsi, Twa; Twa potters
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)
notes: Imigongo origin story (Prince Kakira) is oral tradition.

name: Mapungubwe
making_significance: Mapungubwe elites were buried with gold foil objects including the gold rhinoceros, the earliest known gold-working in southern Africa at this scale.
materials_techniques: gold foil over wooden cores; glass bead trade; ivory
leaves_out: commoners of the valley below the hill; the burials' descendants and apartheid-era silence about the site
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Human remains reburied 2007; do not display burials.

name: Great Zimbabwe
making_significance: Great Zimbabwe's builders raised mortarless granite enclosures and its elites handled gold, copper and imported glass beads and ceramics.
materials_techniques: dry-stone walling; gold working; soapstone carving
functions: rule and display;shelter;exchange and value;ritual and belief
defined_by: archaeologists; colonial writers who denied African authorship
leaves_out: the Shona-speaking makers written out by colonial myth; commoners; the birds removed 1889–91
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: One bird returned from Germany (2003); the site is central to F1.3 historiography.

name: Mutapa
making_significance: Mutapa's rulers controlled gold mining and trade with Swahili and Portuguese merchants in cloth and beads.
materials_techniques: gold mining; alluvial panning; cloth trade
leaves_out: gold miners including women and seasonal workers; captives of Portuguese prazo estates
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Zulu Kingdom
making_significance: Zulu royal authority shaped regimental shields, headrests, beadwork and dress codes.
materials_techniques: cowhide shields; wood carving; glass beadwork
leaves_out: peoples conquered and displaced in the 1820s; women beadworkers; 1879 war loot in British collections
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: "Mfecane" framing contested.

name: Merina Kingdom
date_note: c. 16th c. origins; unification under Andrianampoinimerina c. 1787–1810; French conquest 1895–97
making_significance: The Merina court patronised silk lamba weaving and the timber palaces of the Rova at Antananarivo.
functions: rule and display;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief
leaves_out: enslaved andevo who were a large share of producers; coastal Sakalava, Betsileo and other peoples
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Silk lamba also used as burial shrouds (funerary).

name: Sakalava kingdoms
making_significance: Sakalava royal cults kept relics of past kings (dady) and royal tombs with carved enclosures.
leaves_out: enslaved people traded through Boina; Vezo and other neighbours
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Relic shrines are sacred and active; no display.

name: Kingdom of Kongo
date_note: c.; Portuguese contact 1483; nominal kingdom to 1914
making_significance: Kongo's court and Christian elites commissioned raffia textiles, ivory horns and crucifixes that joined Kongo and Catholic forms.
materials_techniques: raffia pile and embroidered cloth; ivory carving; copper-alloy casting
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;exchange and value
defined_by: Kongo and Portuguese written sources; historians (Thornton)
leaves_out: people enslaved and sold through Kongo's wars and ports; commoner weavers; Mbundu and other neighbours
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)

name: Kingdom of Loango
making_significance: Loango carvers made spiral-relief ivory tusks for European buyers depicting coastal trade, including enslaved people in coffles.
leaves_out: people depicted as captives; the carvers' names; Vili traders
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Tusks show slave coffles: content note.

name: Kuba Kingdom
date_note: c.; founding king Shyaam a-Mbul a-Ngoong c. 1625; kingship continues
making_significance: The Kuba court patronised raffia cut-pile textiles, ndop royal figures and carved cups, with men weaving and women embroidering.
materials_techniques: raffia weaving; cut-pile embroidery; wood carving
object_types: ndop figures; raffia cloths; cups; masks
functions: rule and display;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief;exchange and value
defined_by: Kuba oral histories; Emil Torday; Jan Vansina
leaves_out: subject groups (Kete, Twa); women embroiderers credited only as "Kuba"; colonial collecting
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Luba Kingdom
making_significance: Luba officials used carved lukasa memory boards, staffs and caryatid stools to record and display royal history.
materials_techniques: wood carving; bead and shell inlay
functions: rule and display;record and writing;ritual and belief
defined_by: Luba mnemonic specialists (Mbudye); scholars (Mary Nooter Roberts)
leaves_out: peripheral workshops such as the "Buli Master" (attribution debate); women titleholders
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Mangbetu Kingdom
making_significance: Mangbetu court style shaped harps, anthropomorphic pots and headdresses, many made for colonial-era demand.
functions: rule and display;play and music;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: the Azande and other neighbours; makers producing for collectors
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: "Mangbetu style" partly a colonial-market creation.

name: Bamum Kingdom
date_note: c.; traditional founding; Sultan Ibrahim Njoya r. c. 1889–1933; kingdom continues
making_significance: Njoya created the Bamum script and a palace workshop system for brass casting, beadwork and weaving.
materials_techniques: lost-wax brass casting; beadwork; indigo-resist ndop cloth; Bamum script
object_types: beaded thrones; masks; script manuscripts; maps
functions: rule and display;record and writing;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Grassfields neighbours; the throne Mandu Yenu given to Germany in 1908 (Berlin)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)

name: Kingdom of Benin
date_note: c.; traditional dynasties from 13th c.; British sack 1897
making_significance: Benin's royal guilds of brass casters (Igun Eronmwon) and ivory carvers produced plaques, heads and tusks for the Oba's court.
materials_techniques: lost-wax brass casting; ivory carving; coral beadwork
object_types: plaques; commemorative heads; carved tusks; regalia
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
defined_by: Edo guilds and the Oba's court; historians
leaves_out: guilds as named makers; captives; Edo commoners; the 1897 looting
free_sources: Digital Benin (open data);Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Oba dynasty (continuing) is a DYN row. Digital Benin gives object locations.

name: Ife
date_note: c.; florescence 12th–15th c.; the Ooni continues
making_significance: Ife workshops cast naturalistic copper-alloy heads, modelled terracotta sculpture and made glass beads.
materials_techniques: lost-wax casting of copper and zinc-brass; terracotta; glass bead making
leaves_out: present Yorùbá community; Frobenius's claim of foreign origin
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out);open-access excavation reports

name: Oyo Empire
making_significance: Oyo's cavalry state drew wealth from cloth, horses and the sale of captives, and Shango worship shaped carved staffs.
leaves_out: people sold into the Atlantic trade; tributary Aja and Egba; Hausa and Nupe makers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Asante Empire
date_note: c.; British annexation 1901; the Asantehene continues
making_significance: Asante royal patronage organised gold casting, brass goldweights, kente weaving and adinkra stamping.
materials_techniques: gold casting; brass goldweights; kente strip weaving; adinkra stamping
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;clothing and adornment;ritual and belief
leaves_out: enslaved and tributary peoples; Fante and coastal neighbours; people sold on the coast; objects looted 1874 and 1896
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Golden Stool is sacred and never shown as an exhibit.

name: Dahomey
making_significance: Dahomey's court commissioned appliqué cloths, cast-brass figures by the Hountondji guild and earthen palace reliefs.
functions: rule and display;war;record and writing;ritual and belief
leaves_out: people captured and sold to the Atlantic trade; the Agojie; 1892 French looting (26 objects returned to Benin 2021)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;musée du quai Branly collection search (link out);open-access excavation reports

name: Efik city-states of Old Calabar
making_significance: Old Calabar's Ekpe society used nsibidi signs and indigo-resist ukara cloth as emblems of authority.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
defined_by: historians; Antera Duke's diary; Ekpe members
leaves_out: Igbo dyers who made ukara; people sold through Calabar
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Debated as a polity (houses and society rather than a king). Ekpe knowledge is restricted.

name: Hausa city-states
making_significance: Kano and other Hausa cities ran indigo dye pits, leatherworking and embroidered-robe production traded across the Sahara.
functions: exchange and value;clothing and adornment;rule and display
leaves_out: enslaved workers; Fulani herders; non-Muslim neighbours
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Kofar Mata dye pits' 1498 date is traditional.

name: Sokoto Caliphate
making_significance: The caliphate's cities produced embroidered gowns, manuscripts and leather and expanded slave-based plantation production.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;record and writing
leaves_out: enslaved labour (a large share of the population); non-Muslim neighbours raided
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Library Endangered Archives Programme (link out; terms vary)

name: Kanem-Bornu
date_note: c.; Kanem from c. 9th c.; Bornu from late 14th c.; Rabih's conquest 1893
making_significance: Bornu scholars copied Qur'ans in a distinctive Kanembu hand, and the state traded horses and people across the Sahara.
functions: ritual and belief;record and writing;exchange and value
leaves_out: people enslaved and exported north; Kotoko and other neighbours
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);British Library Endangered Archives Programme (link out; terms vary)
notes: Sayfawa dynasty is a DYN row.

name: Ghana (Wagadu)
date_note: c. 4th? to 13th century CE; dates debated; aligned with CIV007
making_significance: Wagadu's rulers controlled gold and salt exchange described by al-Bakri in 1068.
defined_by: al-Bakri and Arabic geographers; Soninke oral tradition; archaeologists
leaves_out: identification of the capital (Koumbi Saleh) debated; gold producers outside its control
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports
notes: Unrelated to the modern state of Ghana except by name.

name: Mali Empire
making_significance: Mali's rulers funded earthen mosques and scholarship at Timbuktu, and Sahelian gold under their control reached Mediterranean markets across the Sahara.
materials_techniques: earthen architecture; gold trade; manuscript copying
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value;record and writing
defined_by: Arabic writers (al-Umari, Ibn Battuta); griots and the Sunjata epic
leaves_out: enslaved people; nyamakalaw artisan groups (smiths, leatherworkers, griots); non-Muslim subjects
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items);British Library Endangered Archives Programme (link out; terms vary)
notes: Keïta dynasty is a DYN row. Djinguereber attribution to al-Sahili is traditional. Djenné was at most an intermittent tributary of Mali (Tarikh al-Sudan says never conquered), so its mosque is not credited to Mali.

name: Songhay Empire
making_significance: Songhay under Sonni Ali and the Askias ruled Gao and Timbuktu, where the mudbrick Tomb of Askia was built.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: enslaved farming villages; Tuareg and Fulani neighbours
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;British Library Endangered Archives Programme (link out; terms vary);Library of Congress (public-domain items)
notes: Askia dynasty is a DYN row.

name: Mossi kingdoms
date_note: c.; kingdoms continue under the Mogho Naba
making_significance: Mossi political order separated ruling Nakomse from earth-priest groups, and masks belong mostly to the latter.
leaves_out: the Nyonyose (earlier inhabitants) who hold mask traditions; commoners
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Toucouleur (Umarian) state
making_significance: The treasure of Ségou, including Umar Tall's sword, was taken by French troops in 1890 and entered Paris collections.
leaves_out: Bamana and other conquered peoples; the treasure's descendants
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;musée du quai Branly collection search (link out)
notes: Sword attributed to Umar Tall returned to Senegal 2019.

name: Carthage
date_note: traditional foundation date; Roman destruction 146 BCE
making_significance: Carthaginian workshops made glass-paste pendants, terracotta masks and purple dye, and the tophet held carved stelae.
materials_techniques: core-formed glass; terracotta; purple dyeing; stone carving
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Libyan and Numidian subjects; enslaved people; Roman hostile framing
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Tophet interpretation (child sacrifice) debated: handle with care.

name: Fatimid Caliphate
making_significance: Fatimid Cairo's workshops produced lustreware, rock-crystal ewers, tiraz textiles and carved wood.
materials_techniques: lustre ceramics; rock-crystal carving; tiraz embroidery; woodcarving
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment;exchange and value
defined_by: historians; Fatimid sources; Cairo Geniza documents
leaves_out: Christian and Jewish artisans recorded in the Geniza; the Sunni majority; enslaved soldiers and servants
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Fatimid dynasty and polity are the same; no DYN row. Rock-crystal ewers dispersed from the treasury in the 1060s.

name: Mamluk Sultanate
making_significance: Mamluk patrons commissioned enamelled glass lamps, inlaid brass, monumental Qur'ans and endowed complexes in Cairo.
materials_techniques: enamelled glass; brass inlay with silver; illumination; stone architecture
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: the enslaved origin of mamluks themselves; Coptic and Jewish artisans; peasants
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Omani state
other_names: Imamate and Sultanate of Oman; Muscat and Oman
date_note: Ya'ruba expulsion of the Portuguese 1650; state continues
making_significance: The Omani state built forts such as Nizwa and sustained silversmithing, dhow building and an Indian Ocean empire into East Africa.
materials_techniques: silversmithing; dhow building; mudbrick and stone forts
leaves_out: enslaved East Africans on Omani plantations; Baluchi soldiers; Indian merchants
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Qatar Digital Library

name: Teotihuacan
date_note: c.; collapse of centre c. 550 CE
making_significance: Teotihuacan housed craft workshops in apartment compounds producing obsidian tools, pottery, murals and stone masks, and distributed Thin Orange ware made in southern Puebla.
materials_techniques: obsidian knapping; lime-plaster mural painting; moulded ceramics; talud-tablero building
leaves_out: its own name and rulers unknown; foreign barrios (Oaxacan, Maya); present Nahua communities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);LACMA (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons;Mediateca INAH (link out; check terms)

name: Monte Albán (Zapotec state)
making_significance: Monte Albán's elites commissioned carved stone slabs, effigy urns and painted tombs.
materials_techniques: stone carving; moulded ceramic urns; tomb painting
leaves_out: Zapotec villages outside the capital; present Zapotec communities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Mediateca INAH (link out; check terms)

name: Tikal (Mutul)
date_note: c.; dynastic count from c. 90 CE; last dated monument 869
making_significance: Tikal's lords commissioned carved stelae and lintels, painted vessels and temple-pyramids signed by scribes and sculptors.
materials_techniques: limestone carving; sapodilla-wood lintels; polychrome ceramics
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: commoner farmers; captives shown on monuments; present Maya communities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;LACMA (public-domain images)
notes: Tikal's dynasty and polity treated as one row.

name: Kaanul (Snake) kingdom
date_note: c.; seat moved from Dzibanche to Calakmul c. 635
making_significance: The Kaanul kings commissioned codex-style painted vessels and stelae and dominated a network of client lords.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: client cities; commoners; present Maya communities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Dynasty and polity combined here; codex-style vessels heavily looted.

name: Copán
date_note: dynasty founded by Yax K'uk' Mo' 426; last dated monument 822
making_significance: Copán's rulers commissioned high-relief stelae and the Hieroglyphic Stairway, the longest known Maya inscription.
materials_techniques: volcanic tuff carving; stucco; hieroglyphic writing
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: sculptors' workshops as makers; non-Maya neighbours to the east; present Ch'orti' communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Penn Museum collection search (link out)

name: Tula (Tollan)
making_significance: Tula's colonnaded buildings and warrior columns were later idealised by the Mexica, whose word toltecayotl meant fine craftsmanship.
leaves_out: the gap between Mexica legend and archaeology; surrounding Otomí populations
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Mediateca INAH (link out; check terms)
notes: Debated polity; much of "Toltec" is a Mexica retrospective.

name: Mixtec kingdoms
making_significance: Mixtec courts produced screenfold codices, cast gold jewellery and turquoise mosaics exchanged across Mesoamerica.
materials_techniques: deerskin screenfold painting; lost-wax gold casting; turquoise mosaic
functions: rule and display;record and writing;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
defined_by: Mixtec codices themselves; scholars (Caso, Jansen and Pérez Jiménez)
leaves_out: many small ñuu reduced to one label; commoners; present Ñuu Savi communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Mediateca INAH (link out; check terms);British Museum collection search (link out)
notes: Codex Zouche-Nuttall is in the British Museum; images via BM link-out.

name: Mexica and the Triple Alliance
making_significance: Tenochtitlan's tribute system brought feather mosaics, goldwork and textiles to the capital, where amanteca featherworkers and stone carvers served the rulers.
materials_techniques: feather mosaic; stone sculpture; lost-wax goldwork; tribute cloth
object_types: featherwork shields and headdresses; sculpture; codices
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value;war
leaves_out: tributary peoples; the allies Texcoco and Tlacopan; captives; Tlaxcala and other enemies
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;LACMA (public-domain images);Mediateca INAH (link out; check terms)
notes: "Aztec" is a later scholarly label.

name: Tlaxcala
date_note: c.; independent until 1519, then an allied Indigenous province under Spain with privileges until independence
making_significance: Tlaxcalan painters made the Lienzo de Tlaxcala around 1552 to record their alliance with the Spanish.
leaves_out: Tlaxcalans framed as "traitors"; commoners; lost original lienzo
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Mediateca INAH (link out; check terms)
notes: End date approximate; verify.

name: Tarascan state

name: Coclé chiefdoms

free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Penn Museum collection search (link out)

name: Taíno cacicazgos of Hispaniola
making_significance: Taíno chiefs used carved duhos, cemí figures and cotton belts in rituals of authority.

name: Muisca Confederation
making_significance: Muisca goldsmiths cast tunjo votive figures and the Muisca raft by lost-wax in tumbaga.
defined_by: Spanish chroniclers; Museo del Oro; archaeologists
leaves_out: debated as confederation; commoners; present Muisca cabildos
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Moche polities

making_significance: Tiwanaku carved andesite gateways and monoliths, and its ritual networks spread tapestry, snuff trays and keros.

name: Inca (Tawantinsuyu)
date_note: conventional date for Pachacuti; Vilcabamba resistance to 1572

date_note: c.; national council from 1790s; constitution 1827; continues

notes: Debated polity.

date_note: chartered 1670; governed Rupert's Land until 1870; continues as a retailer

name: Viceroyalty of New Granada

making_significance: Palmares was a maroon polity of formerly enslaved people whose settlements produced their own pottery and farmed the Serra da Barriga.

free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;open-access excavation reports

name: Jamaican Maroons
making_significance: Maroon communities who escaped slavery kept the abeng horn, Kromanti ritual and their own drums.

free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;community-published site

name: Haiti
date_note: independence 1804; northern kingdom of Henri Christophe 1811–20
making_significance: Independent Haiti built the Citadelle Laferrière and the Sans-Souci palace and later became a centre of painting and Vodou flag-making.

free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Mexico, post-revolutionary state
making_significance: The Ministry of Education under Vasconcelos commissioned public murals, and the state promoted "arte popular" through the 1921 exhibition and craft policy.
materials_techniques: fresco mural painting; ceramics; lacquer; textiles
leaves_out: Indigenous makers turned into national symbols; women artists; rural producers
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Cuba (revolutionary state)
making_significance: The Cuban state's film institute ICAIC and solidarity organisation OSPAAAL produced screen-printed posters that circulated worldwide.
leaves_out: designers' names under state institutions; censorship
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: United States (federal craft and Indian arts policy)
making_significance: US federal policy both suppressed Native making (boarding schools) and regulated it through the Indian Arts and Crafts Board (1935) and the Indian Arts and Crafts Act (1990).

name: Canada (Inuit art co-operatives)

leaves_out: Inuit authorship under co-op branding; disc-number system; potlatch ban on the Northwest Coast (1884–1951)

name: Danish colonial Greenland

leaves_out: Kalaallit authority over their own economy; East and North Greenland communities
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;SMK Denmark (public domain)

name: Marajoara chiefdoms

free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Tapajó
making_significance: The Tapajó centre at Santarém made caryatid vessels and green-stone muiraquitã amulets traded across Amazonia.
leaves_out: debated as polity; people later enslaved by Portuguese
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Debated polity.

name: Hawaiian Kingdom
making_significance: Hawaiian rulers commissioned feather cloaks and helmets and later Kalākaua revived hula and built ʻIolani Palace.

free_sources: community-published site;Wikimedia Commons;Smithsonian Open Access (CC0 items)

date_note: constitution 1875 under George Tupou I; continues

free_sources: Te Papa Collections Online (CC BY where marked);Auckland Museum Collections Online (CC BY where marked);Wikimedia Commons

name: Bau chiefdom and Kingdom of Viti

notes: Debated polity.

name: Rome (Republic and Empire)

making_significance: Roman production standardised stamped terra sigillata, spread glassblowing and relied on enslaved and freed makers across the provinces.
materials_techniques: glassblowing; terra sigillata; concrete; mosaic; bronze
leaves_out: enslaved and freed makers; provincial peoples; women's work
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Getty Museum Open Content (public-domain images);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Byzantine Empire
making_significance: Byzantine emperors controlled silk production and guilds (Book of the Eparch) and patronised mosaics, icons and enamels.
materials_techniques: mosaic; silk weaving; cloisonné enamel; icon painting
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Jews, Armenians and other subjects; enslaved people; Iconoclasm's losses
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Walters Art Museum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: "Byzantine" is a later label.

name: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms
making_significance: Anglo-Saxon kingdoms produced the Sutton Hoo and Staffordshire hoard metalwork and, with monasteries, the Lindisfarne Gospels.
materials_techniques: gold and garnet cloisonné; manuscript illumination; embroidery
leaves_out: Britons; enslaved people; women embroiderers
free_sources: British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons;British Museum collection search (link out)

name: Early medieval Irish kingdoms
making_significance: Irish kings and monasteries commissioned metalwork such as the Ardagh chalice and manuscripts such as the Book of Kells.
leaves_out: unfree labour; Viking-era captives
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Carolingian Empire
making_significance: Carolingian court schools produced illuminated manuscripts, ivories and the Palatine Chapel at Aachen.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: Saxons converted by force; slaves traded; peasants
free_sources: British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons;Europeana
notes: Carolingian dynasty same as polity.

name: Holy Roman Empire
making_significance: The Empire's courts and free imperial cities, such as Nuremberg, supported goldsmiths, printers and instrument-makers under guild rule.
materials_techniques: goldsmithing; printing; clock and instrument making
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Jews; peasant makers outside guilds; women excluded from mastership
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Europeana;Wikimedia Commons

name: Kingdom of France
making_significance: The French crown under Colbert founded royal manufactures (Gobelins 1662, Sèvres royal from 1759) to set European luxury standards.
leaves_out: enslaved people in French Caribbean colonies; journeymen; women in the trades
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Paris Musées (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Getty Museum Open Content (public-domain images)
notes: Valois and Bourbon are DYN rows.

name: Kingdom of England
making_significance: England's professional embroiderers in London made opus anglicanum vestments exported across Europe.
materials_techniques: silk and gold embroidery; wool trade
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: women embroiderers; Welsh and Irish neighbours; wool producers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;V&A collections search (link out)
notes: Tudor dynasty is a DYN row.

name: Burgundian State
making_significance: The Valois dukes of Burgundy commissioned Flemish tapestries, panel paintings and books of hours from urban workshops.
leaves_out: urban weavers and guild members; rebel cities
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Dutch Republic
making_significance: The Dutch Republic's open art market and guilds produced paintings, Delftware imitating Chinese porcelain, and maps, financed partly by colonial trade.
materials_techniques: oil painting; tin-glazed earthenware; engraving; printing
leaves_out: enslaved people via the West India Company; colonial subjects; women artists
free_sources: Rijksmuseum (CC0);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Link to VOC row.

name: Hanseatic League
date_note: merchant association from 12th c.; first diet 1356; last diet 1669
making_significance: Hanseatic trade carried Lübeck altarpieces, Flemish cloth and Baltic amber and furs, and standardised the cog ship.
leaves_out: Baltic peoples; non-German towns; debated polity
free_sources: Europeana;Wikimedia Commons
notes: Debated polity: a league of cities.

name: Republic of Venice
making_significance: Venice concentrated glassmakers on Murano (1291) under guild secrecy and made the city a centre of printing and lace.
leaves_out: Dalmatian and Greek subjects; enslaved people; glassmakers barred from emigrating
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Republic of Florence
making_significance: Florence's guilds (Arte della Lana, Calimala) organised cloth production and commissioned public art.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: wool workers (Ciompi revolt 1378); enslaved domestic workers; women
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Gallery of Art Washington (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Medici is a DYN row.

name: Papal States
making_significance: Papal Rome ran mosaic and tapestry workshops and commissioned major painting and building.
leaves_out: Jewish community in the ghetto; enslaved galley rowers
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Crown of Aragon
making_significance: Aragon's Valencia and Manises lustreware workshops, many Muslim-run, exported across Europe.
leaves_out: Mudéjar and Morisco makers expelled 1609
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Spanish Empire
date_note: major American losses 1820s; Cuba and Philippines 1898
making_significance: The Spanish empire's silver and trade channelled American and Asian materials into Europe and regulated colonial crafts.
leaves_out: Indigenous and African labour; expelled Jews and Moriscos
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)
notes: Habsburg is a DYN row; viceroyalties are separate rows.

name: Portuguese Empire
making_significance: Portuguese trade commissioned Afro-Portuguese ivories, Namban goods and Indo-Portuguese furniture and ran a large share of the Atlantic slave trade.
leaves_out: people enslaved and transported; colonised makers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: British Empire
making_significance: The empire built art schools, museums and exhibitions (from 1851) and extracted materials and objects across its territories.
leaves_out: enslaved people (trade to 1807, slavery to 1834/38); colonised makers; looted objects
free_sources: British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)
notes: British Raj separate row.

name: French colonial empire
date_note: c.; first empire from 16th c.; second 1830–1962; Vanuatu 1980
making_significance: France's colonial exhibitions (1931) and ethnographic museums displayed objects taken from colonised peoples.
leaves_out: enslaved people in the Caribbean; colonised makers; looted objects (Sarr–Savoy report 2018)
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;musée du quai Branly collection search (link out)

name: German colonial empire
making_significance: German colonial rule gathered large ethnographic collections through war and purchase, and committed genocide in Namibia (1904–08).
leaves_out: Herero and Nama killed in the 1904–08 genocide; Maji Maji dead (1905–07); Cameroonian, Togolese and Pacific makers whose objects fill German museums; Chinese in Qingdao
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Congo Free State and Belgian Congo
other_names: État indépendant du Congo; Congo belge
making_significance: Leopold II's rubber and ivory regime used forced labour and violence, and its collecting built the Tervuren museum.
leaves_out: Congolese forced labourers; mutilated and killed people
free_sources: AfricaMuseum Tervuren collection search (link out);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Content note required.

name: Kyivan Rus'
making_significance: Kyivan princes built Saint Sophia with mosaics and frescoes and patronised cloisonné enamel and icon painting.
leaves_out: Finnic and Baltic peoples; enslaved people traded
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0)
notes: Claimed by Ukrainian, Russian and Belarusian histories.

name: Novgorod Republic
making_significance: Novgorod's birch-bark letters record everyday craft and trade, and its icon painters served a merchant republic.
functions: record and writing;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Finnic tributaries; fur-trade hunters
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Muscovy
other_names: Grand Duchy of Moscow; Tsardom of Russia
making_significance: Muscovite rulers employed Italian architects in the Kremlin and set up the Armoury workshops for icons and regalia.
leaves_out: Tatar and Finnic peoples; serfs
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Russian Empire
making_significance: The empire ran an Imperial Porcelain Factory and court jewellers such as Fabergé and extracted fur tribute (yasak) from Siberian peoples.
materials_techniques: porcelain; enamel and goldsmithing; fur trade
leaves_out: serfs; Siberian and Caucasus peoples; Sámi
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth
making_significance: The Commonwealth's nobility wore silk kontusz sashes woven at Słuck and commissioned coffin portraits.
leaves_out: serfs; Jews, Ruthenians and Tatars
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Europeana

name: Bulgarian Empire (First and Second)
making_significance: The Bulgarian courts at Preslav and Tarnovo produced painted ceramic icons and the Cyrillic writing tradition.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: Slav and Vlach subjects; Bogomils
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons
notes: Gap 1018–1185 under Byzantium.

name: Moldavia
making_significance: Moldavian princes covered monastery churches in Bukovina with exterior frescoes in the 1530s.
leaves_out: Roma enslaved in Moldavia until 1855
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Viking-age Scandinavian kingdoms
making_significance: Scandinavian rulers commissioned rune stones (Jelling), ship burials and carved wood in styles such as Urnes.
leaves_out: enslaved people (thralls) traded widely; Sámi
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;SMK Denmark (public domain);Nationalmuseum Sweden (public domain)
notes: Debated polity.

name: Swedish Empire
making_significance: Sweden's warship Vasa (1628) survives, and its armies took artworks and books such as the Codex Gigas as booty.
leaves_out: Sámi; war victims; looted collections in Stockholm
free_sources: Nationalmuseum Sweden (public domain);Wikimedia Commons

name: Nazi Germany
making_significance: The Nazi state staged propaganda design, "Degenerate Art" (1937) and looting of Jewish and occupied collections, using forced labour.
leaves_out: persecuted Jewish, Roma and other makers; forced labourers
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)
notes: Restitution research central.

name: Soviet Union
making_significance: The Soviet state ran Vkhutemas (1920–30), propaganda porcelain and posters, and reorganised crafts into artels while using Gulag labour.
leaves_out: Central Asian, Caucasus and Siberian peoples; Gulag prisoners; religious makers
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Library of Congress (public-domain items)

name: Republic of Turkey (early reforms)
making_significance: Early republican reforms changed dress (Hat Law 1925), the alphabet (1928) and state textiles (Sümerbank, 1933).
functions: rule and display;record and writing;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: Armenians, Greeks, Kurds; religious crafts
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Emirate and Caliphate of Córdoba
making_significance: Córdoba's Umayyad court workshops at Madinat al-Zahra carved ivory pyxides and enlarged the Great Mosque.
leaves_out: Christian and Jewish makers; enslaved people (saqaliba)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Umayyad dynasty DYN.

name: Nasrid Kingdom of Granada
making_significance: The Nasrid court built the Alhambra and supported lustreware, silk and carved stucco.
materials_techniques: lustre ceramics; silk; stucco carving; tilework
leaves_out: Muslims later converted and expelled; enslaved
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Nasrid dynasty same as polity.

name: Sultanate of Rum
making_significance: Rum's sultans built caravanserais and palaces with figural lustre and underglaze tiles.
leaves_out: Christians; Turkmen nomads
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons
notes: Seljuk dynasty DYN row.

name: Shang
making_significance: Shang foundries at Anyang cast ritual bronzes in piece-moulds and diviners inscribed oracle bones, the earliest Chinese writing.
materials_techniques: piece-mould bronze casting; jade carving; bone inscription
object_types: ding and other vessels; oracle bones; jades
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: human sacrifice victims; foundry labour; non-Shang neighbours (e.g. Sanxingdui)
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data;Wikimedia Commons

name: Western Zhou
making_significance: Western Zhou bronzes carried long cast inscriptions recording grants, and ritual sets defined rank.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: subject lineages; regional states
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data;Wikimedia Commons

name: Chu
making_significance: Chu workshops produced lacquered wood, silk and bamboo-slip texts in a distinct southern style.
materials_techniques: lacquer; silk weaving and embroidery; bamboo slips
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: non-Zhou southern peoples
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Qin
making_significance: The Qin state standardised script, weights and measures, and workshops mass-produced the terracotta army with stamped makers' names.
materials_techniques: modular terracotta production; bronze casting; standardisation
leaves_out: conscripted labourers and convicts; conquered states
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Met Open Access (CC0)

name: Han
making_significance: Han state lacquer workshops inscribed the names of each craftsman on products, and silk and paper spread along its routes.
materials_techniques: lacquer; silk; paper; jade burial suits
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value;record and writing
leaves_out: Xiongnu and southern peoples; convict labour
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Northern Wei
making_significance: The Northern Wei carved the Buddhist cave temples of Yungang and Longmen.
leaves_out: the Xianbei rulers' own language and customs; the labourers who cut the caves; later removal of heads to foreign collections
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Tang
making_significance: Tang workshops made sancai glazed ceramics, silver and silk, and the dated printed Diamond Sutra of 868 survives from Dunhuang.
materials_techniques: sancai glazing; woodblock printing; silver; silk
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;exchange and value
leaves_out: Sogdian and other foreign makers; An Lushan rebels; buried figures
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);British Library digitised collections (public-domain items);Wikimedia Commons

name: Tibetan Empire
making_significance: The Tibetan Empire founded the Jokhang, made silver vessels and ruled Dunhuang (786–848).
leaves_out: conquered peoples of the Tarim and Gansu; Bon practitioners; Chinese and Nepali artisans
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;Himalayan Art Resources (link out)

name: Liao
making_significance: The Khitan Liao made ceramics, silver and polychrome wood sculptures and devised Khitan scripts.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: Han Chinese subjects; Jurchen and other tributaries
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Western Xia
making_significance: The Tangut state printed Buddhist texts in its own script, including early movable-type books.
leaves_out: a state erased by the Mongol conquest; Chinese and Tibetan makers within it
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons;International Dunhuang Programme (link out; check terms)

name: Song
making_significance: The Song state ran official kilns (Ru, Guan) and expanded printing, with Bi Sheng's movable type recorded by Shen Kuo.
materials_techniques: official ceramics; woodblock printing; paper money
functions: rule and display;record and writing;exchange and value
leaves_out: Liao, Xi Xia and Jin rivals; rural and kiln workers; women's textile labour
free_sources: National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data;Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Yuan
making_significance: The Yuan registered artisan households and blue-and-white porcelain with imported cobalt developed at Jingdezhen.
leaves_out: hereditary artisan households; southern Chinese ranked lowest; Persian and Central Asian makers
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);Cleveland Museum of Art Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Ming
making_significance: Ming imperial kilns and Orchard Factory lacquer set standards, and artisan households owed labour service.
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;ritual and belief
leaves_out: hereditary artisan households; kiln workers; Mongol, Jurchen and southwestern peoples
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data;Wikimedia Commons

name: Qing
making_significance: The Qing Imperial Workshops (Zaobanchu) and Canton export trade produced objects for court and global markets.
leaves_out: Dzungars (destroyed 1755–58); Uyghurs and Tibetans; export painters in Canton; the 1860 looting of the Summer Palace
free_sources: Met Open Access (CC0);National Palace Museum Taipei Open Data;Rijksmuseum (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Dian Kingdom
making_significance: Dian bronzes include cowrie containers with cast figural lids depicting rituals.
leaves_out: the Dian's own name for themselves; Han conquest framing
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: People's Republic of China
making_significance: The PRC organised crafts into co-operatives and research institutes, mass-produced propaganda posters, and saw heritage destroyed in the Cultural Revolution.
materials_techniques: poster printing; state ceramics; embroidery co-operatives
functions: rule and display;exchange and value;record and writing
leaves_out: Tibetan, Uyghur and other minority makers; artists persecuted 1966–76
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Goguryeo
making_significance: Goguryeo nobles were buried in stone-chamber tombs painted with murals of daily life, hunting and the four guardian animals.

free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Baekje
making_significance: Baekje workshops made the gilt-bronze incense burner of Buyeo and sent Buddhist craftsmen, tile-makers and texts to Japan.
materials_techniques: gilt-bronze casting; roof tiles; stone pagodas
functions: ritual and belief;rule and display;exchange and value
leaves_out: artisans sent to Yamato under their own names only in Japanese sources
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Silla
date_note: traditional founding; unification of the peninsula's south 668/676
making_significance: Silla goldsmiths made the gold crowns of Gyeongju tombs, and Unified Silla built Seokguram and cast the Divine Bell of King Seongdeok.
materials_techniques: gold sheet and granulation; stone carving; bronze bell casting
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;clothing and adornment
leaves_out: the bone-rank system's commoners; Gaya and Baekje conquered
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Balhae
making_significance: Balhae built capitals with Tang-style roof tiles and Buddhist images in the Manchurian and Russian Far East.
leaves_out: Mohe majority; contested national claims
free_sources: Wikimedia Commons

name: Goryeo
making_significance: Goryeo potters inlaid celadon (sanggam), the state carved the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks, and Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving book printed with metal movable type.
materials_techniques: inlaid celadon; woodblock carving; metal movable type
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: potters of special craft villages (so); Mongol-period tribute women
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Joseon
making_significance: The Joseon court promulgated Hangul (1446), ran official white-porcelain kilns and recorded state rituals in illustrated Uigwe.
materials_techniques: white porcelain; buncheong; illustrated manuscripts; movable-type printing
functions: rule and display;record and writing;ritual and belief
leaves_out: potters taken to Japan during 1592–98 invasions; nobi (unfree) labour
free_sources: National Museum of Korea e-museum (KOGL Type 1);Wikimedia Commons

name: Yamato state (Kofun period)
making_significance: Yamato rulers built keyhole-shaped tombs lined with haniwa and adopted Sue stoneware and techniques from Korean immigrant makers.

free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Nara ritsuryō state
making_significance: The Nara state cast the Great Buddha of Tōdai-ji and stored imported and local objects in the Shōsōin repository.
leaves_out: conscripted labourers; Emishi
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Wikimedia Commons

name: Heian court
making_significance: The Heian court fostered kana writing, yamato-e painting, maki-e lacquer and buildings such as the Byōdōin.
functions: rule and display;ritual and belief;record and writing
leaves_out: provincial cultivators; Emishi
free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

name: Kamakura shogunate
making_significance: Kamakura patronage rebuilt Tōdai-ji with Kei-school sculptors such as Unkei and supported swordsmiths.

free_sources: ColBase Japan (Japan Government Standard Terms);Met Open Access (CC0);Wikimedia Commons

making_significance: The Muromachi state traded with Ming China and fostered Zen ink painting, tea practice and Noh.
